 The Average Retiree Gets $25,000 a Year From Social Security. Here’s Why That Doesn’t Cover Retirement
 Millions of retirees lean on Social Security as their financial foundation, but the numbers behind that plan reveal a gap that catches most people off guard before it's too late to close it.
 By Maurie Backman 
 Published November 3, 2026, 4:02am ET · 3 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 The average retiree collects $25,000 annually from Social Security, covering only 41% of the $61,432 older Americans typically spend each year.
 Social Security's average benefit barely covers housing costs alone, leaving transportation, food, and healthcare expenses largely unfunded.
 Saving $300 monthly starting at age 25 can grow to nearly $933,000 by 65, generating $37,000 yearly to bridge the Social Security gap.

 If there’s one thing financial planners tend to tell clients, it’s “save for retirement from as early an age as you can.” There’s a reason for that.
 There are many retirees today who are living on just Social Security. And people in that situation tend to struggle financially. If you don’t save well for retirement, you could end up being one of them.
 Let’s compare today’s average Social Security benefit to the cost of retirement in America so you can see how important it is to prioritize your savings.
 What the average Social Security benefit pays today — and how it holds up
 The average monthly Social Security benefit tends to rise over time because benefits are eligible for a cost-of-living adjustment each year. As of August 2026, the average monthly Social Security benefit for retirees was about $2,088. When we multiply that benefit by 12, it amounts to a little more than $25,000 a year.
 Now, let’s compare that $25,000 in Social Security to what it costs to be retired today. According to the most recent Consumer Expenditure Survey from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, households led by someone aged 65 or older spend an average of $61,432 annually.
 Here’s how that spending breaks down:
 Housing: $22,193 annually
 Transportation: $9,538 annually
 Food: $7,940 annually
 Healthcare: $7,799 annually
 The remaining $14,000 (roughly) covers retirees’ remaining expenses.
 This suggests that the typical Social Security benefit today covers only about 41% of the average older American’s spending. So if your plan is to retire on Social Security alone, you should know that if you’re eligible for the average benefit, it may not cover much more than housing.
 Don’t set yourself up for a financially stressful retirement
 If you don’t want to spend your senior years struggling financially, it’s important to do what you can to save for retirement. The good news is that you don’t need to part with tons of money every month to build up a large nest egg over time. You just need to consistently fund a retirement account from a young age and let your investment portfolio do the rest.
 Let’s imagine you start saving $300 a month for retirement at age 25 and continue to do so until you turn 65. If you invest that money heavily in stocks, your portfolio might deliver an 8% annual return, which is slightly below the market average.
 Your total balance in that scenario? Almost $933,000.
 Now, if we apply the popular 4% rule to a savings balance of $933,000, that would give you another $37,000 a year in retirement plan withdrawals. Combine that with $25,000 a year in Social Security, and you have enough money to spend what the average older American does on annual living expenses.
 Without those retirement account withdrawals, though, the numbers fall apart. So while it’s fine to factor Social Security into your retirement income plan, living on those monthly checks alone is not a smart idea. You may not even be able to afford a basic lifestyle if you don’t save any money at all.
